newsitem.title: USA: Sparks CEO pegs U.S. corn output at 9.3-9.4 bln bu.
newsitem.headline: Sparks CEO pegs U.S. corn output at 9.3-9.4 bln bu.

text.p: Sparks Companies President and Chief Executive Officer Carrol Brunthaver on Monday estimated U.S. final corn production at 9.3 to 9.4 billion bushels.
That figure was above the U.S. Agriculture Department's November 1 estimate for 9.265 billion bushels.
Brunthaver, speaking at a National Grain and Feed Association conference, said ending corn stocks would total 1.1 billion bushels.

Abundant corn supplies and shrinking export markets will likely erode corn futures prices in the coming months, Brunthaver added. He predicted December 1997 Chicago Board of Trade futures prices would fall to between $2.40 to $2.45 a bushel this spring.

"Corn, I'm a little negative on," he said, adding that weather would always be the wild card. Given normal growing conditions, Brunthaver said corn supplies at the end of 1997 could reach 11 billion bushels.
Large world supplies will also weigh on U.S. soybean exports and prices next spring, Brunthaven said.
The production estimate was higher than Sparks' November estimate of 9.142 billion bushels.
Brunthaver also predicted U.S. corn exports would fall by as much as 350 million tonnes next year as large world grain supplies fed traditional markets.
He said good growing conditions in countries like Spain, China and South Korea will drastically reduce their corn import needs.
"We should write them off as an importer (next year)," Brunthaver said, referring to China.

Brunthaver said China had probably completed its soybean and soymeal purchases for the year. Also, Brazil and Argentina were forecasting record soybean crops which would likely attract buying interest from Pacific Rim countries.
He pegged U.S. soybean ending stocks at 175 million bushels, compared with last year's ending stocks of 180 million bushels.
U.S. wheat markets were also expected to struggle as world supplies grow, he said. He noted that U.S. stocks remained tight and not competitive with Argentine, Australian and European supplies.
He predicted July CBOT futures would trade belew $3.00 per bushel during harvest next summer.
